item.title: PCS to Fort Carson: A VA Loan Home Buying Guide for Colorado Springs
item.dc:creator: Brandon Armstrong
item.description: Moving to Fort Carson on PCS orders? Learn how VA loans, the COE, and the funding fee work, and how to time a Colorado Springs home search to your orders.
item.content:encoded:
If you have PCS orders to Fort Carson, you can buy a home in Colorado Springs with a VA-backed loan, and many buyers do it with no down payment. The steps that matter most are requesting your Certificate of Eligibility early, getting pre-approved with a lender who closes VA loans regularly, and timing your search around your report date. Here's how I walk military buyers through it.

VA loan basics for Fort Carson buyers

A VA-backed purchase loan is made by a private lender and backed by the VA. According to the VA's purchase loan page, you may be eligible if you qualify for a Certificate of Eligibility (COE), meet the VA's and your lender's standards for credit and income, and plan to live in the home. The same page says these loans often offer:

  • No down payment, as long as the sales price isn't higher than the appraised value
  • No private mortgage insurance (PMI)
  • Fewer closing costs, which the seller may pay
  • No penalty for paying the loan off early

The VA doesn't set your interest rate. Your lender does, so it's worth comparing more than one lender before you commit.

Start with your COE

Your COE confirms to the lender that you qualify for the VA home loan benefit. The VA's COE page says you can request it online, through your lender, or by mail. Active-duty service members need a statement of service signed by their commander, adjutant, or personnel officer. Veterans need their DD214. If you can, get this done before you leave your current duty station.

Understand the funding fee

Most VA buyers pay a one-time VA funding fee, which you can pay at closing or roll into the loan. The VA's funding fee page says the fee is a percentage of the loan amount based on your loan type, whether it's your first use, and your down payment. As of the VA's current chart, a first-use purchase loan with less than 5% down carries a 2.15% fee. Buyers who receive VA compensation for a service-connected disability are among those who don't pay it.

The same page says the VA limits seller concessions to 4% of the home's reasonable value, and that the funding fee can be financed into the loan or paid at closing. Your lender's Loan Estimate is the place to confirm your actual numbers.

Planning your search around your orders

Fort Carson sits on the south side of Colorado Springs, and its relocation team notes that more than 60% of the active-duty military population lives in the local communities. That gives you real options, from neighborhoods on the south and southeast side of the Springs to the City of Fountain and areas farther north if you're willing to commute.

Here's the order I usually recommend:

  1. Get your COE and a VA pre-approval as soon as your orders are in hand.
  2. Figure out your move-in window, including any time you'll spend in temporary lodging.
  3. Start touring remotely with video walkthroughs so you're ready to act when you arrive.
  4. Line up inspections and the VA appraisal with closing dates that fit your report date.

Fort Carson's Army Community Service also runs a monthly virtual homebuyers workshop, and the Housing Services Office on post can point you to rental and housing resources. Both are worth using alongside your own agent and lender.

Questions to ask before you make an offer

These are the questions I go over with every PCS buyer:

  • How long do I expect to be stationed here, and would I keep this home as a rental after my next move? (Ask your lender and a tax professional about the rules that apply to you.)
  • What will my commute to my gate actually look like at rush hour?
  • Does the home need repairs that could hold up the VA appraisal?
  • Is the home in an HOA or special district, and what do those fees cover?

Military and PCS moves are a big part of what I do. I've spent 10+ years in business with 200+ transactions closed in Colorado Springs and the surrounding areas, and I know how much a tight report date can squeeze a home search. You can read more on my military and PCS page or reach out when your orders come through.

VA loan rules can change. Confirm your eligibility, fees, and loan terms with your lender and VA.gov.

Bottom Line

If you have PCS orders to Fort Carson, request your COE early, get pre-approved with a lender who knows VA loans, and plan your search around your report date. I'm happy to help you map out the move.

item.title: Old Colorado City vs. Downtown vs. Fountain: Colorado Springs Guide
item.dc:creator: Brandon Armstrong
item.description: Comparing Old Colorado City, Downtown Colorado Springs, and Fountain? Here's the history, landmarks, and practical questions to weigh before you buy a home.
item.content:encoded:
Old Colorado City, Downtown Colorado Springs, and Fountain each give you a different version of life in the Pikes Peak region. Old Colorado City is a historic west-side neighborhood, Downtown is the original core of Colorado Springs, and Fountain is a separate city next to Fort Carson. The right fit comes down to your commute, the kind of home you want, and what you want close by.

Old Colorado City: El Paso County's first permanent settlement

Old Colorado City started as its own town. According to the Colorado Springs Pioneers Museum, Colorado City was the first permanent settlement in El Paso County, founded in 1859 as a trade supply post along Fountain Creek. Its voters approved joining Colorado Springs, and the annexation took effect on June 10, 1917.

That history is still easy to see. History Colorado notes that the Old Colorado City Historic Commercial District was added to the National Register of Historic Places on November 2, 1982. It runs along the north side of Colorado Avenue from 24th Street, with examples of Queen Anne, Italianate, and Romanesque Revival architecture among its 27 properties. The City of Colorado Springs adds that the commercial district was almost torn down in the 1970s before local activists saved it.

If you're looking here, I'd pay attention to:

  • Age of the home. If you're looking at an older house, a thorough inspection matters, and so does budgeting for updates.
  • Street parking and lot size. These vary a lot from block to block, so tour in person.
  • Proximity to the Colorado Avenue shops, if being near that district is part of the appeal for you.

Downtown Colorado Springs: the city's original core

Downtown is where Colorado Springs began. The Downtown Partnership says Acacia Park, at the center of Downtown, is the city's first park, donated by city founder Gen. William Jackson Palmer in 1871. Downtown also has America the Beautiful Park in the southwest corner, with access to the Midland and Pikes Peak Greenway trails, and Alamo Square Park, which surrounds the Colorado Springs Pioneers Museum.

Southwest Downtown is also home to the U.S. Olympic & Paralympic Museum. Its fact sheet says it opened to the public on July 30, 2020, in a 60,000-square-foot building.

Things to think about Downtown:

  • Home type. If you're shopping condos, lofts, or townhomes, read the HOA documents closely.
  • Parking and storage. Ask whether a unit includes a garage space or a storage unit.
  • Event activity. Parks and venues host events throughout the year, so visit on a weekend evening, not just a quiet weekday morning.

Fountain: its own city next to Fort Carson

Fountain isn't a Colorado Springs neighborhood. It's a separate city with its own city hall on Main Street. The City of Fountain says the town was founded in 1859, the same year as Colorado City, and incorporated as a town in 1903. The Fountain Trading Company building, established in 1898, still stands at 117 Main Street. Fort Carson was founded in 1942 and has been Fountain's neighbor ever since.

For military buyers, that location is a big part of the draw. Fort Carson's relocation team notes that the post's Carson Connector shuttle runs in partnership with City of Fountain Transit.

When I help buyers compare Fountain, we look at:

  • Commute. Drive the route to your gate or your job at rush hour before you commit.
  • Taxes, fees, and services. Fountain is a separate city, so compare its property taxes, HOA or special district fees, and utility providers with Colorado Springs addresses.
  • Different parts of town. Tour a few areas of Fountain rather than judging the whole city from one street.

I've spent 10+ years in business and closed 200+ transactions in Colorado Springs and the surrounding areas, and I'm always glad to show buyers these three areas side by side. See more on my neighborhoods page, or read my Fort Carson PCS buying guide if you're moving on orders.

Bottom Line

Old Colorado City and Downtown put you inside Colorado Springs near its oldest landmarks, while Fountain is its own city next to Fort Carson. Tour all three at different times of day before you decide.
